label: Royal Charter of the Bank of England
summary: 27 July 1694: William & Mary grant a charter to a private company that will lend £1.2m to fund war with France. The public-good clause still echoes in the Bank’s mission.

label: Opens at Mercers’ Hall
summary: 1 August 1694: business begins in rented rooms in Cheapside with ~17 clerks. An experiment in war finance, not yet the ‘Old Lady’.

label: Sir John Houblon, first Governor
summary: Houblon’s early years are dominated by government cash needs, new coinage, and accepting public deposits—central banking before the name exists.

label: Early discounting & Bank Rate
summary: From 1695 the Bank’s discount rate becomes a measurable price of liquidity—sticky at first, but already a policy-ish instrument.

label: Great Recoinage crisis
summary: Clipped silver is withdrawn; coin shortage hits trade. The young Bank is strained by redemptions while still lending for war.

label: Newton becomes Warden of the Mint
summary: Isaac Newton is appointed Warden (1696) and helps drive the recoinage’s engineering and anti-counterfeiting work—science meets the money stock.

label: Specie payments under strain
summary: War lending plus recoinage pressure brings an early near-death experience: notes vs metal under fiscal stress.

label: Capital enlargement & tallies
summary: The Bank absorbs short-term government paper (tallies), binding it more tightly to national-debt machinery.

label: Savery’s steam pump patented
summary: Thomas Savery patents a steam pump for mines—an early industrial power idea that Newcomen will soon make practical.

label: Newton Master of the Mint
summary: Newton becomes Master (1699–1727). He stays a working Mint administrator and counterfeiting hunter while remaining Europe’s celebrity natural philosopher.

label: Act of Union — one fiscal state
summary: England and Scotland unite; London’s debt market becomes the financing engine of a larger British state.

label: Six-partner rule on note banks
summary: Legal scaffolding restrains large partnership banks of issue—early privilege that will evolve toward note monopoly.

label: South Sea Company chartered
summary: A rival debt manager with empire trade privileges (incl. asiento) threatens the Bank’s government-finance franchise. Consol yields spike near war peaks (~8.7% annual average this year).

label: War-finance yield peak
summary: Long British yields around the War of the Spanish Succession hit their early-century high—state credit priced as expensive and scarce.

label: Newcomen’s atmospheric engine
summary: Thomas Newcomen’s engine drains mines with atmospheric pressure and steam—first commercially successful heat engine, years before Watt.

label: Peace of Utrecht & debt overhang
summary: War ends; the problem shifts from wartime cash to managing a permanent national debt through London markets.

label: Newton’s mint ratio — de facto gold
summary: As Master of the Mint, Newton helps set the guinea toward 21s. Relative metal prices push Britain toward a de facto gold standard.

label: South Sea scheme beats the Bank
summary: Parliament chooses the South Sea Company’s debt-conversion plan over the Bank’s rival bid (Feb). Stock price begins its mania climb.

label: Newton sells South Sea — books a profit
summary: In late April Newton liquidates most South Sea holdings (sale orders ~19 & 23 Apr). Odlyzko estimates ~£20,000 profit on the early stake—not the oft-cited £7,000 alone.

label: Bubble peak, Newton re-enters, crash
summary: Prices soar into summer; Newton appears to rebuy heavily (incl. converting other securities). September collapse. Mid-1721 net worth ~£20k vs ~£30k+ pre-bubble; family lore’s £20k loss is plausible, archival estimate often ~£10–14k opportunity loss.

label: ‘Madness of the people’
summary: Earliest sourced version (Spence via Lord Radnor): when asked if the rise would continue, Newton said he ‘could not calculate the madness of the people.’ The ‘motions of the heavenly bodies’ flourish was added by later writers.

label: Parliamentary inquiry & survivors
summary: Inquiry exposes fraud and politics. The South Sea model is humbled; the Bank’s government-debt role consolidates.

label: Partially printed banknotes
summary: Notes for £20+ begin with printed denominations (cashier still completes the amount)—standardisation after pure holograph paper.

label: Threadneedle Street premises
summary: Purpose-built home on the site the Bank still occupies. Institutional presence becomes architecture.

label: Jacobite scare & liquidity
summary: Political shock tests note confidence and City credit as Bonnie Prince Charlie’s rising reaches England.

label: Consols consolidated
summary: Scattered perpetual debts are tidied into ‘consols’—the benchmark long bond of the British state for generations.

label: Calendar reform (Britain skips 11 days)
summary: Britain adopts the Gregorian calendar. Quiet administrative science that remaps the civic year markets settle on.

label: Seven Years’ War begins
summary: Global war financed through London’s debt markets with the Bank at the centre of government cash.

label: Harrison’s H4 chronometer trial
summary: John Harrison’s marine chronometer proves longitude at sea is solvable—empire navigation meets precision craft, after the Longitude Prize decades.

label: Peace of Paris — empire enlarged
summary: Victory expands British claims; the bill is paid in consols and taxes. Yields ease from wartime pressure.

label: Hargreaves’s spinning jenny (c.)
summary: Hand-powered multi-spindle spinning spreads in Lancashire—textile productivity that will demand factories, credit, and cotton trade.

label: Watt’s separate-condenser patent
summary: James Watt patents a method to cut steam waste (5 Jan 1769). With Boulton later, it becomes the workhorse of industrial power.

label: Arkwright’s water frame
summary: Richard Arkwright’s water-powered spinning patents industrialise yarn—mills, capital, and new labour regimes follow.

label: Ayr Bank crash
summary: Scottish failure transmits into London—early modern pattern of regional credit crunch hitting the centre.

label: American war finance begins
summary: Fiscal stress rises without yet breaking convertibility; London still prices the empire’s quarrel in sterling debt.

label: Wealth of Nations + Watt engines at work
summary: Adam Smith publishes; Boulton & Watt engines start commercial service. Ideas and machines arrive together in the Bank’s century.

label: Cornwallis surrenders at Yorktown
summary: Military defeat; the debt remains. Peacemaking will still leave a larger peacetime fiscal state.

label: Peace of Paris — American independence
summary: War ends; consol yields stay elevated vs mid-century lows as markets digest lost colonies and debt stock.

label: Soane appointed Bank architect
summary: John Soane begins a 45-year rebuild—fortress walls and interiors that define Threadneedle Street until the 20th century.

label: War with Revolutionary France
summary: Military-fiscal state shifts into overdrive; gold drains accelerate toward the Restriction crisis.

label: Jenner’s cowpox inoculation
summary: Edward Jenner demonstrates vaccination against smallpox—public-health tech that will reshape labour and cities in the industrial century.

label: Restriction Period begins
summary: 26 Feb: Privy Council orders the Bank to stop paying notes in gold after invasion panic drains reserves (~£16m→~£2m in contemporary BoE telling). Wartime paper by necessity.

label: ‘Old Lady of Threadneedle Street’
summary: Gillray’s ‘Political Ravishment’ caricature of Pitt wooing the Bank’s gold popularises the nickname that sticks.

label: Low-denomination notes flood out
summary: £1 and £2 notes compensate for missing coin—and meet an often-illiterate public, priming a forgery epidemic.

label: Consol yields near wartime highs
summary: Annual long yields ~5.9% (BoE/FRED)—markets price invasion risk and paper money together.

label: National debt on a war footing
summary: Debt stock climbs toward Waterloo-scale mountains; consols are the thermometer of state survival.

label: Trafalgar — sea power, debt power
summary: Naval victory protects trade routes; the fiscal capacity behind the fleet is the Bank’s partnership with Parliament.

label: Bullion Committee report
summary: Intellectual fight: is the high price of gold ‘too many notes’? Currency vs banking arguments that will haunt Peel’s generation.

label: War of 1812 & Continental strain
summary: Another theatre of expense while Restriction continues—sterling paper finances a world war.

label: Stephenson’s Blücher locomotive (c.)
summary: Early steam locomotives appear on colliery lines—railways will soon become both tech boom and securities mania.

label: Waterloo & the bill for victory
summary: Victory financed; peacetime politics of returning to gold begins. Yields still ~5% annually.

label: Coinage Act — gold de jure
summary: Legal gold standard framed even before full convertibility returns.

label: Resumption Act (Peel’s first gold push)
summary: Parliament schedules a return to cash payments—defining 19th-century monetary choice.

label: Convertibility restored
summary: Gold payments resume at parity. Restriction ends after 24 years. Classical standard era begins in earnest.

label: Faraday’s electromagnetic rotation
summary: Michael Faraday demonstrates the principle of the electric motor—laboratory physics that will later wire markets and messages.

label: Country-bank panic
summary: Classic run/liquidation crisis after Latin American and domestic speculation. BoE learns crisis lending under fire.

label: Stockton & Darlington Railway opens
summary: First public steam railway—tech that will demand capital markets and, within two decades, a railway mania.

label: First BoE branches
summary: Gloucester opens 19 July 1826 (and others follow)—geographic note control after country-bank failures.

label: Stephenson’s Rocket wins Rainhill
summary: Locomotive contest proves speed and reliability—railways become investable technology, not curiosity.

label: Liverpool & Manchester Railway
summary: First inter-city passenger steam railway. Capital, land, and labour rearrange around iron schedules.

label: Faraday discovers electromagnetic induction
summary: Induction makes generators and dynamos conceivable—the physics under eventual telegraph and power industries.

label: Bank Charter renewal politics
summary: Privileges renegotiated; notes edge toward legal-tender status in England. Public-interest framing hardens.

label: Mid-cycle credit strains
summary: Instability in the late 1830s helps motivate the rules of 1844.

label: Telegraph patents & Cooke–Wheatstone
summary: Electric telegraphy becomes commercial in Britain—information speed that will change market microstructure.

label: Daguerreotype / Talbot photography
summary: Photography is announced to the world—a new way to document crises, people, and the Bank’s own fortress.

label: Bank Charter Act (Peel’s Act)
summary: 19 July 1844: Issue vs Banking departments; fiduciary issue capped; path to English note monopoly. Rules over discretion—until panic.

label: Currency School vs Banking School
summary: The Act enshrines bullionist rules. The long argument behind modern central banking is now statute.

label: Bank Rate cut to 2.5%
summary: Days after the Act, the Bank cuts rate historically low (never below 4% since founding, per contemporary comment)—new regime, new tools.

label: Railway Mania peak
summary: Parliaments authorise vast railway capital; share frenzy and fraud. Tech boom and securities bubble are the same story.

label: Repeal of the Corn Laws
summary: Free-trade turn reshapes prices, politics, and the City’s global role—money meets political economy.

label: Crisis — Act suspended
summary: Commercial crash; Chancellor’s letter lets the Bank exceed the fiduciary limit. Proof that 1844 breaks in panic.

label: Irish Famine & fiscal limits
summary: Hunger meets monetary orthodoxy debates—empire and sterling rules collide with catastrophe (historians still argue how much the Act constrained relief).

label: European revolutions & City nerves
summary: Political upheaval across the Channel; London prices risk while remaining the settlement centre.

label: Great Exhibition
summary: Crystal Palace showcases industrial Britain—tech confidence on a gold-standard stage.

label: Bessemer converter
summary: Henry Bessemer’s process enables cheap bulk steel—rail, ships, and bridges get a new material basis.

label: Global panic hits London
summary: Atlantic transmission from US failures; Act suspended again. Classical standard under stress.

label: Discount-window discipline on brokers
summary: Bank restricts bill brokers’ routine access—early moral-hazard push that will haunt 1866.

label: First lasting Atlantic cable attempt era
summary: Transatlantic telegraphy is attempted (success solidifies in the mid-1860s)—markets begin to share news at cable speed.

label: Darwin’s Origin of Species
summary: Natural selection published in London. Victorian science’s own ‘shock’—pepper for a money timeline that claims to be about a world, not only ledgers.

label: Rate politics vs bill brokers
summary: Conflicts over Bank Rate in dividend season—the politics of the discount window before Bagehot’s book.

label: US Civil War & cotton famine
summary: Lancashire distress and Atlantic finance; London remains the clearing house of a divided trade world.

label: London Underground opens (Metropolitan)
summary: World’s first underground passenger railway—urban tech financed in the same City that prices consols.

label: Mendel / Pasteur era biology (select)
summary: Germ theory and experimental biology mature on the Continent while London’s money markets modernise—parallel revolutions.

label: Overend, Gurney fails — Black Friday
summary: 9–10 May: Bank refuses the insolvent discount house; panic follows; Act suspended; Rate to 10%. Defining LOLR stress test.

label: Transatlantic cable in regular service
summary: Reliable cable links London and New York—finance and news compress. Same year as Overend: wires and runs together.

label: Chancellor’s letter & Rate 10%
summary: Suspension authorises notes beyond gold backing; high Rate is the price of the rules break—doctrine still contested.

label: Suez Canal opens
summary: Shortcut to Asia remaps trade times and insurance—empire logistics that sterling credit underwrites.

label: Chief Cashier sole note signature
summary: George Forbes becomes the only signatory—iconic authority convention still on notes today.

label: German Empire & gold scramble
summary: Franco-Prussian settlement and German monetary unification intensify Europe’s move toward gold—London’s standard goes global.

label: Bagehot’s Lombard Street
summary: Canonical doctrine: in panic, lend freely on good collateral at a high rate. Theory catches practice.

label: Maxwell’s Treatise on Electricity
summary: James Clerk Maxwell states field equations that unify light and electromagnetism—pure science peak of the Victorian century.

label: Continental / US strains
summary: 1873 panic waves through Vienna and New York; London as gold settlement centre absorbs transmission.

label: Bell’s telephone patented
summary: Telephone era begins—voice at distance joins telegraph in remaking how orders and rumours move.

label: City of Glasgow Bank failure
summary: Unlimited-liability shock; joint-stock banking reforms accelerate. Note and deposit trust under gold.

label: Edison / Swan electric light
summary: Practical electric lighting races ahead—infrastructure that will need capital on a new scale.

label: Classical gold standard zenith (c.)
summary: Sterling/London clearing as global public good—with empire asymmetries. Consol yields grind lower.

label: Edison’s Pearl Street / electric utilities
summary: Central-station electricity becomes a business—another industry for City finance to price.

label: Benz motorwagen / auto dawn
summary: Petrol carriage patents—future tech still fringe, but the invention pepper belongs on a long money-world timeline.

label: Goschen conversion of the debt
summary: Interest on consols cut (toward 2¾ then 2½)—Victorian confidence written into the coupon. Yields ~2.8%.

label: Michelson–Morley / modern physics cue
summary: Null ether-drift result unsettles classical physics—science timeline pepper beside a calm consol market.

label: Kodak camera — snapshot culture
summary: Mass photography democratises images; crises and crowds will be easier to document than in 1825.

label: Baring crisis lifeboat
summary: Lidderdale organises a syndicate rescue of Barings after Argentine exposure—SIFI playbook before the acronym.

label: Gold drain without announcing a break
summary: Crisis management protects convertibility without a theatrical rules suspension—confidence theatre matters.

label: Consol yields ~2.7%
summary: Despite Baring, annual long yields stay low by 18th-century standards—Victorian ‘cheap money’ world.

label: Aftermath & Argentine echo
summary: International lending risk is priced back into London; the lifeboat’s moral is debated for decades.

label: First women clerks (Janet Hogarth)
summary: Hogarth becomes first Superintendent of Women Clerks—labour history inside the fortress.

label: Bank’s bicentenary quiet confidence
summary: Two centuries on: the Bank is assumed background of Victorian prosperity—until the next century breaks gold.

label: Röntgen’s X-rays
summary: Invisible light that sees through flesh—fin-de-siècle science flourish as consol yields near their Victorian trough.

label: Consol yields ~2.30% — cheap sterling
summary: BoE/FRED annual average ~2.30%: the long decline from wartime 6–8% to Victorian calm is complete. State credit has never looked safer on this chart.

label: Dow Industrial Average begins (US)
summary: Charles Dow starts publishing the Industrial Average in New York. London still prices the classical gold world—but US equity modernity now has its own continuous index. (Companion story: The Dow, 1896–2026.)

label: Victoria’s Diamond Jubilee & late gold calm
summary: Empire pageantry atop ~2.5% consol yields. Classical gold-standard sterling still looks permanent—an illusion the next half-century will shatter.

label: Thomson’s electron & Marconi’s wireless
summary: J.J. Thomson identifies the electron (Cavendish); Marconi’s radio work accelerates. Physics and telecom begin to remake markets’ information speed.

label: Boer War finance begins
summary: South African war expenses hit the Exchequer. Consols tick up from Victorian lows as colonial war meets peacetime debt habits.

label: Marconi’s Atlantic wireless signal
summary: December 1901: claimed transatlantic radio “S” from Cornwall to Newfoundland. Empire communication starts escaping the cable monopoly.

label: Boer War ends — debt digest
summary: Peace of Vereeniging. War costs absorbed into the gilt market; sterling’s gold link still holds.

label: Wright Flyer — powered flight
summary: Kitty Hawk proves controlled powered flight. Within a generation air power and air mail will rewrite logistics and war finance.

label: US Panic of 1907 hits London
summary: New York’s crash transmits through sterling balances and commodity houses. The Bank manages liquidity while gold still rules.

label: Blériot flies the Channel
summary: Louis Blériot’s Dover landing collapses the English Channel as a mental moat—and foreshadows air-age vulnerability.

label: Rutherford’s nuclear atom
summary: Manchester experiments reframe the atom as mostly empty space with a dense nucleus—physics that will later power both energy and weapons.

label: July–August financial crisis
summary: War outbreak freezes markets; Stock Exchange closes; runs threaten. The Bank and Treasury scramble for emergency liquidity.

label: Gold convertibility effectively suspended
summary: Practical end of peacetime gold payments as reserves and confidence buckle. The classical standard cracks in days.

label: Treasury £1 & 10s notes
summary: Currency and Bank Notes Act: government “Bradbury” notes replace gold coin in pockets—war money for a mass public.

label: War Loan & hidden Bank underwriting
summary: Huge War Loans finance the Allied effort. Later research shows the Bank quietly absorbed stock to fake “oversubscription” confidence.

label: Somme year — fiscal total war
summary: Industrial slaughter meets industrial debt. Consols and War Loans price a conflict with no Victorian precedent.

label: US enters — sterling’s partner shifts
summary: American entry and dollar credit reshape Allied finance. London remains the clearing house, but power tilts west.

label: Armistice — victory & debt mountain
summary: Fighting stops; the bill does not. National debt and inflated prices set the stage for the bitter gold-parity debate.

label: Votes for women (partial) & labour politics
summary: Representation of the People Act widens the franchise. Mass democracy will constrain how hard future Chancellors can squeeze for gold.

label: Cunliffe Committee: restore gold at parity
summary: Official orthodoxy: return to pre-war gold parity ASAP. The policy choice that will define the 1920s.

label: Eddington’s eclipse — relativity confirmed
summary: Sobral/Principe eclipse observations make Einstein world news. Science’s prestige soars just as monetary orthodoxy digs in.

label: Montagu Norman becomes Governor
summary: Norman (Governor 1920–44) personifies interwar central banking—secretive, internationalist, and eventually Treasury-constrained.

label: Postwar yield spike (~5.4%)
summary: Long yields jump as inflation, debt overhang, and deflation politics collide. Consols no longer whisper “Victorian calm.”

label: BBC begins radio broadcasts
summary: British Broadcasting Company starts. Mass media will later amplify runs, rumours, and Chancellor speeches in real time.

label: Return to gold at pre-war parity
summary: Churchill’s decision: sterling back to $4.86. Keynes warns of overvaluation; export industries pay the price.

label: Germany’s Locarno moment — paper peace
summary: European rapprochement on paper while gold orthodoxy rebuilds. Capital flows, not just treaties, hold the system.

label: General Strike — industrial politics
summary: Nine-day general strike after coal lockout. Light beat: class conflict as the underside of gold-parity deflation.

label: Fleming observes penicillin
summary: Alexander Fleming notices mould killing bacteria at St Mary’s. Medicine’s freeroll will reshape labour, longevity—and wartime survival odds.

label: Currency & Bank Notes Act consolidates
summary: Fiduciary issue rules tidied as the gold exchange world matures—paper still promises metal in principle.

label: Wall Street Crash ripples to the City
summary: October crash starts a global credit unwind. London feels it through commodities, Empire debtors, and confidence.

label: Sterling crisis & leave gold
summary: 21 September: Britain abandons the gold standard. The classical project dies; floating sterling begins a new monetary era.

label: National Government formed
summary: Political emergency meets financial emergency. Policy shifts from defending parity to managing recovery.

label: Consols still ~4.4% — then relief
summary: Annual long yield ~4.4% in the crisis year; 1932 Conversion and cheap money then pull rates down as sterling floats.

label: War Loan conversion & cheap money
summary: Massive conversion of 5% War Loan cuts debt service. Bank Rate and gilt yields fall—depression-era monetary easing.

label: Ottawa & the sterling area
summary: Imperial preference and a sterling bloc replace gold’s automatic discipline for much of the Empire/Commonwealth.

label: Watson-Watt radar breakthrough
summary: British radar work accelerates. Detection tech will matter as much as gold reserves when the next war arrives.

label: Keynes’s General Theory
summary: Keynes publishes the book that reframes demand, unemployment, and what central banks & Treasuries think they can do.

label: WWII war finance begins
summary: September: Britain at war again. Exchange control, War Loans, and Treasury direction intensify—Bank as agent of total war.

label: Exchange Control Act toolkit
summary: Capital and currency controls become the peacetime-to-wartime switchboard for sterling.

label: Dunkirk & existential fiscal stakes
summary: Military near-catastrophe; financial survival still runs through US credit, Empire resources, and domestic compulsion.

label: Lend-Lease — dollar lifeline
summary: US Lend-Lease eases Britain’s dollar shortage. Victory finance becomes transatlantic, not purely City-centred.

label: Colossus & Bletchley codebreaking
summary: Electronic cryptanalysis at Bletchley Park. Computing’s wartime birth sits beside sterling’s wartime controls.

label: Bretton Woods agreed
summary: IMF & World Bank designed; dollar–gold hub replaces sterling’s old centrality. Britain signs into a US-led monetary order.

label: D-Day — war’s fiscal endgame starts
summary: Normandy opens the European endgame; planning for reconstruction finance is already underway.

label: War ends — debt, controls, Labour
summary: Victory with a exhausted balance sheet. Attlee’s government inherits rationing, debt, and a Bank still privately owned on paper.

label: Penicillin mass production pays off
summary: Wartime scale-up of antibiotics saves lives on a statistical scale—science’s dividend from the same years as Bretton Woods.

label: Bank of England nationalised
summary: Bank of England Act 1946: private shareholders out; the Bank becomes a public institution. In practice, Treasury primacy was already real.

label: Keynes dies; postwar settlement hardens
summary: April: Keynes dies after negotiating US loans and Bretton Woods details. The intellectual and institutional settlement outlives him.

label: Convertibility crisis
summary: Brief restoration of current-account convertibility drains dollars in weeks. Controls slam back; sterling’s weakness is public.

label: Manchester Baby — stored-program computer
summary: First working stored-program electronic computer runs in Manchester. UK computing pedigree is real—even as US capital scales the industry.

label: Marshall Plan dollars arrive
summary: European Recovery Program eases the dollar gap. Reconstruction finance is American-led; the City adapts.

label: Sterling devalued to $2.80
summary: September devaluation under Stafford Cripps. A blunt admission that wartime/postwar parity hopes were gone.

label: Watson & Crick — DNA structure
summary: Cambridge double helix paper. Molecular biology’s founding image—British lab, global science.

label: Suez & sterling pressure
summary: Military adventure meets financial reality: US pressure and reserve drains force a climb-down. Politics and the pound intertwined.

label: Calder Hall — first civil nuclear power
summary: World’s first commercial-scale nuclear power station opens in Cumbria. Energy tech as national prestige project.

label: Bank Rate to 7% — crisis hike
summary: Defence of sterling and inflation fears push Bank Rate sharply higher—stop-go policy in action.

label: Non-resident convertibility restored
summary: External convertibility for non-residents marks a step out of postwar exchange-control darkness (residents still constrained).

label: Radcliffe Report on the monetary system
summary: Committee questions simple money-supply fetishism; emphasises credit, liquidity, and wider financial structure.

label: M1 motorway opens
summary: Modern motorway Britain begins—oil, cars, and suburban finance will reshape the real economy the Bank tries to steer.

label: Basel / IMF support for sterling
summary: Recurring sterling crises bring central-bank swaps and IMF politics into the open. The reserve-currency burden bites.

label: Wilson incomes policy & stop-go
summary: Labour tries to manage wages, growth, and the peg simultaneously. The Bank operates inside a politicised demand-management machine.

label: Sterling devalued to $2.40
summary: Wilson’s “pound in your pocket” devaluation. Another forced reset of the external value of sterling.

label: Pulsars discovered (Cambridge)
summary: Jocelyn Bell Burnell / Hewish detect pulsars—radio astronomy triumph from British instruments.

label: Gold Pool collapses
summary: Two-tier gold market ends the official Gold Pool defence. Bretton Woods’ gold leg is limping.

label: Concorde first flight
summary: Anglo-French supersonic prototype flies. Prestige tech with a bill that mirrors other national champions.

label: Apollo 11 — Moon landing
summary: US moonshot captures the world’s attention. Tech optimism peaks just as the monetary order is about to break.

label: Competition & Credit Control
summary: CCC reforms aim to replace ceilings with market-based credit control—and unleash competition among banks.

label: Decimal Day
summary: 15 February: pounds, shillings, pence become decimal. Everyday money units finally modernise.

label: Nixon shock — Bretton Woods ends
summary: US closes the gold window. The dollar–gold hub dies; floating rates and inflation become the new normal.

label: Sterling floats
summary: Pound leaves the Smithsonian tunnel toward a float. Exchange-rate politics replace gold orthodoxy for good.

label: UK joins the EEC
summary: European Economic Community membership begins. Trade and later ERM politics will haunt sterling strategy.

label: Oil shock & secondary banking crisis starts
summary: Oil prices explode; property/fringe-bank excesses unwind. The Bank’s “lifeboat” for secondary banks begins.

label: Secondary banking lifeboat deepens
summary: Fringe banks and property loans keep failing. The Bank coordinates rescues while inflation accelerates.

label: Inflation peak — consols ~14.6%
summary: Long yields scream into the mid-teens. The Victorian 2% world is a museum piece; inflation dominates the chart.

label: Secondary crisis winds down
summary: Lifeboat operations gradually stabilise the fringe. Regulatory lessons feed later supervision debates.

label: IMF crisis — Britain borrows
summary: Sterling crisis forces an IMF programme. National humiliation narrative meets monetary conditionality.

label: Concorde enters commercial service
summary: Supersonic passenger service begins—glamour tech against a backdrop of IMF austerity politics.

label: Winter of Discontent begins
summary: Strikes and unburied rubbish become the political symbol of 1970s breakdown—framing Thatcher’s 1979 win.

label: Thatcher wins — monetarist turn
summary: Conservative government elevates money-supply targets and disinflation. The Bank’s operating world changes.

label: Exchange controls abolished
summary: End of postwar capital controls. Sterling and the City reopen to global capital flows.

label: Medium-Term Financial Strategy
summary: MTFS publishes money and fiscal paths. Monetarism as published dashboard—even when targets prove slippery.

label: Consol yields still ~12%
summary: Disinflation is painful: long rates remain in double digits even as policy turns. The chart’s mountain is still high.

label: BBC Micro & home computing boom
summary: BBC Computer Literacy Project puts micros into schools and bedrooms—UK tech culture wave.

label: Reserve-ratio regime loosened
summary: Formal reserve requirements fade further as market operations dominate liquidity management.

label: Miners’ strike — politics of disinflation
summary: Year-long strike becomes the hinge of industrial power vs monetary/fiscal resolve. Light beat only.

label: Domain Name System & networked PCs
summary: Internet naming and personal computers mature together—plumbing for the later WWW boom.

label: Plaza Accord — dollar/sterling politics
summary: G5 intervention agreement to weaken the dollar. Exchange-rate management among majors is back in vogue.

label: Big Bang — City deregulation
summary: 27 October: fixed commissions, open outcry, and clubby ownership rules explode. Electronic trading and universal banks remake London.

label: Single European Act signed
summary: Deeper EC market integration—background pressure toward ERM and eventual euro debates.

label: Black Monday crash
summary: Global equity crash. Central banks ease; the City’s post–Big Bang machine gets its first stress test.

label: Lawson boom accelerates
summary: Credit and house prices surge. Shadowing the Deutschmark and late-80s optimism set up the ERM trap.

label: Tim Berners-Lee proposes the WWW
summary: At CERN, a British engineer drafts the World Wide Web. Information costs for markets are about to collapse again.

label: Berlin Wall falls — geopolitics shift
summary: Cold War’s European endgame. Capital, Germany, and ERM politics will all feel the aftershock.

label: Sterling joins the ERM
summary: October: pound enters the Exchange Rate Mechanism. A hard external constraint returns—without gold’s old mystique.

label: Thatcher resigns
summary: Leadership crisis ends the Thatcher era; Major inherits ERM membership and a slowing boom.

label: BCCI closed by the Bank
summary: Bank of Credit and Commerce International shut. Supervision credibility and “home/host” gaps under scrutiny.

label: WWW software released publicly
summary: Berners-Lee’s tools go public—the web leaves the lab. Within years, markets will trade on browser time.

label: Black Wednesday — exit ERM
summary: 16 September: speculative attack forces Britain out of the ERM. Billions spent; Bank Rate hiked then reversed. Credibility crisis.

label: Bank Rate spike then retreat
summary: Emergency Rate rises fail to defend the peg; policy pivots to floating and later inflation targeting.

label: Consol yields ~9.2% — post-crisis easing path
summary: Long yields still high vs Victorian history, but the inflation mountain is descending from the 1970s peak.

label: Inflation-targeting framework begins
summary: Post-ERM regime: explicit inflation target and warmer Bank–Treasury reporting. Prelude to operational independence.

label: Tricentenary — 300 years of the Bank
summary: July 1994: tercentenary symposium, St Paul’s thanksgiving with the Queen, commemorative £2. The Old Lady marks three centuries.

label: Houblon £50 note issued
summary: Commemorative £50 featuring first Governor Sir John Houblon—bookend to 1694’s charter story.

label: Next: path to operational independence
summary: Epilogue card only: full operational independence arrives in 1997 under Brown—just outside this timeline’s frame. The tricentenary Bank is still Treasury’s agent on rates.
